slides.title: The loop: how a model writes an answer
slides.summary: The model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and runs again on the longer text. It stops when its best guess is the end token.
body: Give the model “The pizza is ready” and ask what comes next. Each run of the model does the same job: turn the text into vectors, pass them through the transformer's layers, and score every possible next token. The second figure below shows one run in full.

ul: Run 1 reads “The pizza is ready” and picks “ for”.
Append it. The input is now “The pizza is ready for”, one token longer.
Run 2 reads all of that, including the word it just wrote, and picks “ you”. Then “!”, one token per run.

body: <mark>The model never writes a whole answer at once. Every token comes from a full run over everything so far, including the tokens it has already written.</mark>

body.h: How does it know it's finished?

body: It doesn't decide in any deep sense. Every answer in its training data ended with a special end token, so once a reply looks complete, that token becomes the most likely prediction. When it wins, the loop stops.

ul: The end token wins: the usual way a reply ends.
A length limit: the app caps the number of tokens, which can cut a reply off mid-sentence.
A stop sequence: the app can also stop when a chosen piece of text appears.

body.text: Inside every run, attention lets the newest token look back at everything before it. That's what makes the model's guesses fit the context, and it's the subject of the next chapter.

body.more: Isn't re-reading the whole text every run slow?
body.text: It would be. Models keep the work already done for earlier tokens in a KV cache, so each run only has to compute the newest token.
body.link: The KV cache in Output & inference

body.more: What does the end token look like?
body.text: It's one of the tokenizer's special tokens, such as <|endoftext|> in GPT-2. Chat models use an end-of-turn token from their chat template.

steps.caption: The model gets the token IDs of the text so far.

figure.alt: The generation loop for "The pizza is ready". Run 1 reads The, pizza, is, ready and predicts " for" at 42%; it is appended. Run 2 reads the five tokens and predicts " you" at 58%; appended. Run 3 reads six tokens and predicts "!" at 47%; appended. Run 4 reads "The pizza is ready for you!" and predicts the special end token at 81%, so the loop stops and the reply is finished. Finishing is just one more prediction: answers in training ended with an end token, so the model learns to predict it once a reply is complete. Apps also stop at a length limit. Probabilities are illustrative.
figure.caption: Each run's winner joins the input for the next run. The reply ends when the end token wins.

figure.alt: How an LLM predicts the next token for "The pizza is ready". 1: split into tokens The, space pizza, space is, space ready. 2: look up token IDs, 791, 23317, 374 and 5644 in GPT-4. 3: turn IDs into vectors of numbers, plus position. 4: run the transformer: N identical layers, each with layer norm, self-attention, where ready looks back at every earlier token, layer norm and a feed-forward network; then layer norm and linear plus softmax, giving one score per vocabulary token. Self-attention is the subject of the next chapter. 5: score every possible token, for 42%, to 31%, at 12%, now 6%, and pick one, giving The pizza is ready for. 6: add it to the text and run again, one token at a time. Values are illustrative.

slides.title: GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformer

ul: A transformer is a type of neural network architecture designed to process sequences of information using attention.
It was introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need”.
Before transformers, sequence models commonly used architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs, which processed text more sequentially.

body: In 2017, Google researchers published “Attention Is All You Need”. Their transformer reads all the tokens at once, and attention links any two words directly, however far apart they are.

slides.title: Why transformers need attention
slides.summary: A word's meaning depends on the words around it. Attention lets each word look at the others and decide which ones matter.
body: For every word, attention answers one question: which other words should I focus on right now, and how much?

ul: “The cat sat on the mat, because it was tired.” Here “it” is the cat.
“…because it was cozy.” Now “it” is the mat.
“…because it was cold weather.” Now “it” is the weather.

body: Self-attention means attention between tokens of the same text: each token looks at the other tokens around it and works out how they relate.
<mark>Without attention, a word looks the same wherever it appears. With it, the surrounding words decide what it means.</mark>

ul: I went to the bank to deposit money. → a place for money
I sat on the bank of the river. → the side of a river

body.text: Each token makes a query, a key and a value, scores every pair and blends the values by those scores. The Attention chapter walks through it step by step.

figure.alt: Attention lets a word look at the other words in its sentence; thicker lines mean more attention. In "The cat sat on the mat, because it was tired", "it" attends most to "cat" (0.71), so it means the cat. With "cozy", "it" attends most to "mat" (0.66). With "cold weather", "it" attends most to "weather" (0.58). In "I went to the bank to deposit money", "bank" attends to "money" and "deposit": a place for money. In "I sat on the bank of the river", "bank" attends to "river": the side of a river. Weights are illustrative.
figure.caption: The highlighted word decides what “it” and “bank” mean. Attention is how the model finds that word.

slides.title: Token + position: building the model's input
slides.summary: Each token gets two vectors: one for what the word is, one for where it sits. Add them, stack the results, and you have the matrix the transformer reads.
body: Before the transformer can do anything, every token has to become a list of numbers. That takes two lookups and one addition.

body.h: Step by step, for “The cat sat”

ul: 1 · Token IDs. The tokenizer turns the text into numbers, for example The → 791, cat → 8415, sat → 7731.
2 · Token embedding: what. Each ID picks its row from the token table, which holds one learned vector per word in the vocabulary. “cat” always gets the same row.
3 · Position embedding: where. Each slot picks a row from the position table: one vector for position 0, one for position 1, and so on. “cat” sits in position 1, so it gets row 1.
4 · Add. Add the two vectors number by number: first plus first, second plus second. The result has the same length.

body.note: How the adding works: a position vector always has the same length as a token vector: the model's width. Line the two up and add slot by slot: 1st + 1st, 2nd + 2nd, and so on. In GPT-2 both have 768 numbers, so the input has 768 too. Its position table has 1,024 rows, one per position, which is why GPT-2 can read at most 1,024 tokens.

body: <mark>The transformer never sees the word and its position separately. It gets one vector per token that carries both.</mark>

body.note: Like a place card at a wedding: one card with the guest's name and their table number. Same guest, different table, different card.

body.h: The input is now a matrix

body: Stack the three sums on top of each other, one row per token, and you get a grid of numbers: a matrix. Here it has 3 rows (tokens) and 4 columns (numbers per token), so its shape is [3, 4].

ul: Rows grow with the text. A 1,000-token prompt makes 1,000 rows.
Columns are fixed by the model. GPT-2 uses 768 numbers per token; Llama 3 8B uses 4,096.

body: <mark>This matrix is the whole input. The transformer reads all its rows at once, and every layer passes on a matrix of the same shape.</mark>

body.more: Why add them instead of putting them side by side?
body.text: Joining the two vectors end to end would double their length and make every layer bigger and slower. Adding keeps the size the same. With hundreds or thousands of numbers per vector there's room for both kinds of information, and training learns to keep them apart.

body.note: Is this RoPE? No. Adding a position vector is how GPT-2 worked. Most modern models use RoPE instead, covered on the next slide.

body.more: Why does word order need this at all?
body.text: Without position, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give the model the same three vectors.

viz.html: One row per token, one column per number: shape [3, 4]. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: For “The cat sat”, each token looks up its token embedding (what the word is) and its position embedding (where it sits), and the two are added number by number. For cat in position 1: [0.2, −0.4, 0.7, 0.1] + [0.1, 0.3, −0.2, 0.4] = [0.3, −0.1, 0.5, 0.5]. The three input vectors are stacked into a 3 by 4 input matrix that goes into transformer layer 1. Below: cat in position 1 and cat in position 5 give different input vectors. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Two lookups and one addition per token, then the rows are stacked into the input matrix.

slides.title: RoPE: how modern models add position
slides.summary: Instead of adding a position vector, RoPE turns each token's vector by an angle that depends on its position.
body: Most modern models, including Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and DeepSeek, don't add a position vector at the input. They use RoPE, short for rotary position embedding.

ul: Picture a token's vector as an arrow.
Position 0: no turn. Position 1: turn a little. Position 2: turn twice as much, and so on.
The arrow keeps its length, so the meaning is kept. Only its direction changes, and that shows where the word sits.

body: <mark>When attention compares two words, what matters is the angle between them. That angle depends only on how far apart they are.</mark>

Take “The cat sat” from the last slide: The is position 0, cat is 1, sat is 2. cat and sat are one step apart. If the same words appear again at positions 101 and 102 in a long story, they're still one step apart, so they get the same angle.

body.note: Two friends on a merry-go-round: wherever the ride turns, the angle between them stays the same.

body.text: Inside attention, in every layer, on the query and key vectors that attention uses to compare tokens. The token's own vector is never changed. Attention, the next chapter, explains queries and keys.
RoPE tells the model “three tokens back”, not “token 1,207”. That suits language, where nearby words usually matter most. It's also one reason context windows can be made longer after training.

body.more: Why do the pairs turn at different speeds?
body.text: Fast pairs make nearby positions look clearly different. Slow pairs change gradually over long distances. Together they tell the model how far apart words are, both close up and across a long text.

cells.text: how far apart two words are
capped by the table (1,024 in GPT-2)

viz.html: A worked example: “cat” at position 1 in “The cat sat”. Only the direction changes. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: RoPE turns each token by an angle that depends on its position. The word cat, drawn as an arrow, is not turned at position 0, turned 35 degrees at position 1, 70 at position 2 and 105 at position 3. Its length, the meaning, stays the same. Below, for “The cat sat”: cat at position 1 and sat at position 2 are 35 degrees apart, and the same words later in a long story, at 101 and 102, are also 35 degrees apart. Same gap, same angle, wherever the words are. Angles are illustrative.
figure.caption: Turn by position: the angle between two words shows how far apart they are.

slides.title: Layer normalization: keeping the numbers steady
slides.summary: Before each main step, every token's vector is rescaled to a standard range, so the numbers don't grow too big or shrink too small as they pass through many layers.
body: The input matrix passes through dozens of layers, and each layer adds to its numbers. Left alone, they drift: some grow huge, others shrink towards zero, and training becomes unstable.

body.h: What it does to one token

ul: 1 · Subtract the average of the token's numbers, so they're centred on 0.
2 · Divide by the spread, how far the numbers typically sit from the average, so they have a standard size.
3 · Scale and shift with numbers learned in training, so the model can still pick the best range for each slot.

text: The spread is the standard deviation: roughly, how far the numbers typically sit from their average. For “cat” [6, −2, 10, 2]:

1 · Average: (6 − 2 + 10 + 2) ÷ 4 = 4.
2 · Distance of each number from the average: [2, −6, 6, −2].
3 · Square them, so negatives don't cancel positives: [4, 36, 36, 4].
4 · Average the squares: 80 ÷ 4 = 20.
5 · Square root, to undo the squaring: √20 ≈ 4.47.
A small spread means the numbers are bunched together; a large one means they're scattered. Dividing by it gives every token a spread of 1.

body: <mark>Each token is normalized on its own, using only its own numbers. However big or small it comes in, it goes out in the same steady range.</mark>

body.note: Why it matters: normalization keeps the neural network's internal representations well behaved, which makes training deep networks more stable.

text: Mostly no. A vector's meaning is in its pattern, which numbers are high and which are low, and normalization keeps that exactly. It only removes the overall size.

The original is kept. In modern models (GPT-2 onwards, Llama), the norm works on a copy going into attention or the feed-forward step. The token's own vector keeps its full values, and each step adds its result back onto it. The original 2017 Transformer normalized the main vector itself, after each step; moving the norm before each step made deep models easier to train.
The size can come back. The learned scale and shift in step 3 let the model stretch each slot back to whatever range is useful.
One small loss: [6, −2, 10, 2] and [60, −20, 100, 20] look the same to the step reading the copy. The sizes aren't gone, though: they stay in the token's own vector, and models do use them.

body.note: Like the volume control on a microphone: whether the singer whispers or shouts, the level going to the speakers stays steady, and the song stays the same.

body: Inside every transformer layer, just before attention and just before the feed-forward step, plus once more at the very end, before the model predicts the next token.

body.text: The original Transformer and GPT-2 use LayerNorm, as shown here. Most modern models, including Llama, Mistral and Qwen, use RMSNorm, which skips step 1 and only divides by the typical size of the numbers. It's slightly cheaper and works just as well.

viz.html: Try ten times bigger, [60, −20, 100, 20]: the average is 40, the spread 44.7, and the result is exactly the same. Values are illustrative.

figure.alt: Layer normalization for one token. “cat” going in is [6, −2, 10, 2], average 4 and spread 4.47. The same token times 10 is [60, −20, 100, 20], average 40 and spread 44.7. LayerNorm subtracts the average and divides by the spread, and both come out as [0.45, −1.34, 1.34, −0.45], average 0 and spread 1: the pattern is kept, only the size changes. Below, where it sits: input matrix, norm, attention, norm, feed-forward, repeated N times (12 in GPT-2, 32 in Llama 3 8B), then a final norm, then predict the next token. Values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Same pattern, steady size: a norm before each main step, and one at the end.
